title: Nine Months to Save Gumroad's Series B, and the Year Alone After
dek: In 2015 Sahil Lavingia gave his team nine months to reach the numbers for new funding; when they fell short he chose to shrink Gumroad rather than close it.

story.event: Failing to raise a Series B, laying off most of the staff and running Gumroad almost alone
story.summary: In January 2015 Sahil Lavingia told Gumroad's staff of about twenty that they had nine months to reach the growth needed for a Series B. They fell short; rather than shut down and return investors' money, he laid off most of the team in late 2015, launched a premium plan and made the company profitable by mid-2016, for a time running it alone.
paragraphs: In January 2015, at Gumroad's first all-hands meeting of the year in San Francisco, Sahil Lavingia told his team of about twenty that the road ahead would be hard. The company's bank balance had just dipped below eighteen months of runway, and it did not have the numbers to raise a Series B. They had nine months to get close. If they succeeded, they would raise money and hire again; if not, Gumroad would have to shrink drastically.

Lavingia had built Gumroad, a way for creators to sell directly to their audiences through simple links, over a weekend in 2011, then left his job as Pinterest's second employee before his stock vested. In 2012 he raised $1.1 million and then $7 million in a round led by Kleiner Perkins. Sales kept rising, but not at the doubling pace venture investors wanted; he later dated the stall to November 2014 and concluded that too few creators needed what Gumroad offered. Kleiner, he said, led a bridge of about $2 million to pay for the extra months.

Nobody left during those nine months, he wrote, and the team shipped weekly payouts, payouts to Britain, Australia and Canada, and much more. The numbers still fell short. Some investors urged him to shut down, return the money and try for something bigger, and he tended to agree. But he held himself accountable to creators, employees and investors, "in that order", and thousands of creators were being paid through Gumroad every month. In November 2015 TechCrunch reported that Gumroad, with 22 staff earlier that year, was laying off most of them. "This was the hard decision. I didn't want to make one and then six months from now make another," he said.

About five people stayed, and as they found other work the crew dwindled to Lavingia alone. Each day he answered every support query himself, sometimes asking former engineers for help with bugs. He did not tell his mother about the layoffs; she read about them. Lower costs and a new premium plan made Gumroad profitable by June 2016, he recalled. In 2019 he wrote that he had failed to build a billion-dollar company, and that Gumroad had sent $178 million to creators.

quote.text: Who is it that does not voluntarily exchange his health, his repose, and his very life for reputation and glory, the most useless, frivolous, and false coin that passes current amongst us?
quote.locator: Book I, chapter XXXVIII, "Of Solitude" (I.39 in most modern editions)
quote.translator: Charles Cotton (1685), ed. W. C. Hazlitt
quote.source_title: Essays of Michel de Montaigne — Complete, tr. Charles Cotton, Project Gutenberg eBook #3600
quote.connection: Montaigne calls reputation a false coin that people pay for with their health and rest. Lavingia had measured himself by a billion-dollar valuation; giving it up cost him a team and a public image, and by his own account it took years before he stopped calling what was left a failure.

reflection: The decision Lavingia is remembered for is the layoff. The harder stretch, by his own account, came afterwards: months alone, answering every support query himself and keeping the news even from his mother. What he had lost was a measure of success he believed he had inherited from "a society that worships wealth".

You will carry measures of your own, and some of them borrowed. A few will be useful. But a measure kept in secret grows heavier, and saying plainly how things stand, to one person who cares about you, is often how you begin to choose a better one.
invitation: Tell one person close to you how your work is really going this week, including the part you have been keeping to yourself. Then let that be enough for today.

cross_checks.claim: Gumroad laid off most of its staff in late 2015 after failing to grow fast enough to raise new funding on good terms
The team numbered about twenty (22 by TechCrunch) before the layoffs
Gumroad raised $1.1 million and then a $7 million round led by Kleiner Perkins in 2012
In January 2015 Lavingia told the team they had about nine months to reach Series B numbers
About five people remained after the layoffs; the crew later shrank to Lavingia alone

research_notes: Headcount: Lavingia's essay says a 20-person team shrank to five (75 per cent laid off); Mixergy has '20-ish' people and Lavingia plus four others afterwards; TechCrunch (November 2015) reported 22 employees earlier in 2015 and around 3 expected to remain, possibly a little more. The story says 'about twenty', notes TechCrunch's 22, and uses 'about five' remaining from Lavingia's two accounts. The later shrinking to one person rests on Lavingia's own essay (also syndicated by The Next Web), so it is attributed to him. Money raised: the essay gives $1.1 million plus $7 million (2012) and TechCrunch about $8 million, but the essay later speaks of '$10 million of investor capital'; in Mixergy Lavingia describes a 2015 bridge of about $2 million led by Kleiner Perkins plus money from Mark Cuban, which reconciles the totals. The story gives the 2012 rounds and attributes the bridge to Lavingia. Creator payouts: the essay's 'About $2,500,000' is not clearly a monthly figure and Mixergy has processing of 'around $2 million a month', so the story gives no figure and says only that thousands of creators were paid monthly. Burn: Mixergy's title and Lavingia give about $350,000 a month, later about $300,000 in operating costs cut to about $40,000; not used. First profit: June 2016, about $10,000 that month (Mixergy); the essay shows June 2016 financials without the figure; the story says only 'profitable by June 2016'. The cumulative $178 million to creators appears in both the essay and Mixergy (early 2019). TechCrunch's 2015 headline is 'Layoffs Hit Gumroad As The Payments Startup Restructures' at the live URL; Lavingia quotes it as '...E-Commerce Startup Restructures', probably an earlier headline. Montaigne's line comes from his argument that most people's busy lives are spent for reputation rather than for themselves; applied here by analogy.
